problem: Zero-shot embodied navigation agents (e.g. 3D-Mem, VLFM) mostly remember visited regions or hand raw frontier snapshots to a VLM, so they underuse frontier boundaries as exploration cues. They also make overconfident, premature decisions.
motivation: Frontiers link the agent's current state to unseen, potentially goal-relevant areas and shape future trajectories and observations. Explicitly estimating frontier utility, keeping it in a spatio-temporal memory, and double-checking answers should give better long-horizon planning and calibrated decisions.
key_idea: Use a VLM to score each frontier snapshot's exploration potential, propagate the scores into a spatio-temporal potential graph for planning, and validate memory-based goal selections with a self-reconsideration loop.
insight: Potential scores are informative on their own: replacing frontier images with text descriptions plus scores gave performance on par with full SCOPE and better than vanilla frontier images. Removing the potential graph lowers GOAT-Bench SR from about 70.1 to 66.9 and SPL from 52.4 to 47.0, so accumulated spatial-temporal memory matters. Reconsideration confirmations are correct 80.6% of the time, and forced-through rejected answers are wrong 34.3% of the time. ECE also drops (GOAT-Bench 11.62 to 3.83).
method: Frontier-level potential estimator: a prompted VLM (GPT-4o) scores each frontier snapshot on semantic richness, explorability and goal relevance, then aggregates them into a scalar potential P_i.

Potential graph: a 2D grid memory whose cells store potential, visit count and the three semantic scores. Each frontier observation is propagated to cells within radius R with linear distance-decay weights and an exponential-moving-average style update.
Exploration value: E = (w_pot*P + w_sem*p_sem + w_explore*p_explore + w_goal*p_goal) / (1 + gamma*visits), which penalizes revisits; the scores are put in the VLM prompt alongside frontier snapshots.
Self-reconsideration: when the policy picks a memory snapshot-object pair, a VLM validator returns CONFIRM or REJECT. On REJECT the policy is re-queried with the rejected action, up to a retry limit.
Base system: built on the 3D-Mem codebase (snapshot memory plus frontier snapshots, panoramic RGB-D, GPT-4o as decision VLM).

setting.observation: panoramic egocentric RGB-D (1280x1280, HFOV 120, camera height 1.5 m, tilt -30 deg)
setting.action_space: choice of a memory snapshot/object or a frontier snapshot, executed by a low-level planner (3D-Mem style)
setting.privileged: none stated (depth and pose from the simulator)

numbers.eval_set_note: subset as in 3D-Mem (not specified in this paper)

numbers_note: The split names for GOAT-Bench (assumed val-unseen) and A-EQA (val) are not stated in the paper. The ablation numbers are given only in a figure, apart from the values quoted in the text. Five-run means: GOAT-Bench SR 70.1±1.9, SPL 52.4±1.5; A-EQA score 57.5±1.6 and efficiency 39.2±1.8 in the appendix table (the text gives 52.37 for A-EQA correctness).
results: SCOPE reaches 73.7 SR / 53.5 SPL on GOAT-Bench, beating 3D-Mem (69.1 / 48.9). On A-EQA it reaches 59.1 correctness versus 52.6 for 3D-Mem, with efficiency 41.0 slightly below MTU3D (42.6). It also has lower run-to-run variance and better calibration.
limitations: Relies on a strong proprietary VLM (GPT-4o); weaker VLMs fail (Qwen-Omni-Turbo SR 17.27) and repeated VLM calls add cost.
Statistical significance is weak on A-EQA (p=0.1365), and the gains are smaller on the whole GOAT-Bench set (66.8 vs 62.9).
Evaluated only in simulation on two benchmarks, with no real-robot tests.
